summary: Specifies RIPng, a routing protocol for IPv6 internets, based on the algorithms already widely used by RIP in IPv4. It is a simple distance-vector protocol for smaller networks.

plainLanguage.summary: RIPng lets routers in an IPv6 network tell each other which destinations they can reach and how far away they are. Each router sends its whole list to its neighbours every 30 seconds, and every route entry carries a 128-bit IPv6 address prefix. The protocol is small and simple, so it suits small and medium networks rather than large ones.

questions: what is the ripng multicast address
how does ripng send route updates
subtitle: RIP carried over to IPv6: the same simple distance-vector routing, with 128-bit prefixes in each route entry.

tldr.problem: IPv6 networks needed an interior routing protocol, and the IPv4 protocol RIP could not carry 128-bit IPv6 prefixes.
tldr.mechanism: RIPng keeps RIP's distance-vector algorithm, its 30-second periodic updates and its metric limit of 15, but sends 20-byte route table entries over UDP port 521 to the multicast group FF02::9.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard on the standards track with the same limits as RIP: moderate-size networks, a diameter of at most 15 hops and fixed metrics.

today: RFC 2080 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. It describes version 1 of the protocol and says nothing about later versions.

sections.title: Why RIPng Exists
sections.content:
RIPng is a routing protocol for an IPv6 internet. The RFC calls it the minimum change to the Routing Information Protocol (RIP) of RFC 1058 and RFC 1723 that is needed to run over IPv6.

RIPng belongs to the class of algorithms known as distance vector algorithms, also called Bellman-Ford or Ford-Fulkerson algorithms. A router running RIPng keeps a routing table with one entry for every destination reachable in the network. Each entry holds the IPv6 prefix of the destination, a metric that is the total cost of reaching it, the IPv6 address of the next router on the path, a route change flag and timers.

RIPng was designed to work as an Interior Gateway Protocol, a protocol used inside one Autonomous System, in moderate-size networks. The RFC lists three limits. The longest path, the network diameter, is 15 hops when each network costs 1, and larger costs make that ceiling harder to reach. The protocol depends on counting to infinity to resolve some unusual situations, which can be slow or costly in a large looped network. And it uses fixed metrics, so it cannot choose routes by measured delay, reliability or load.
sections.plainLanguage: RIPng is a way for routers to tell each other which places they can reach and what each place costs to reach. Every router sends its list to its neighbours every 30 seconds, and each entry names an IPv6 address prefix and a cost. It is meant for small and medium networks inside one organisation.

sections.title: The RIPng Message Format
sections.content:
RIPng runs over UDP. Every router that uses RIPng sends and receives datagrams on UDP port 521, the RIPng port. All routing update messages are sent from that port, and unsolicited updates use it as both the source and the destination port. A reply to a request goes back to the port the request came from. A specific query may come from another port, but it must be aimed at port 521 on the target machine.

The message starts with a 4-byte header holding a command, a version and two bytes that must be zero. Version 1 is the version described here. Two commands exist: 1 is a request for all or part of the responder's routing table, and 2 is a response carrying all or part of the sender's table. The rest of the datagram is a list of route table entries.

Each route table entry is 20 bytes: a 16-byte IPv6 prefix, a 2-byte route tag, a 1-byte prefix length between 0 and 128, and a 1-byte metric. The metric runs from 1 to 15, and the value 16 means infinity, that is, the destination is not reachable. The route tag is an attribute that must be preserved and readvertised with the route. Its intended use is to separate internal RIPng routes from external routes imported from another protocol.

The next hop address is not carried in every entry, because that would nearly double the size of the entry. Instead a special entry carries it. It is marked by 0xFF in the metric field, and its prefix field holds the next hop IPv6 address. It applies to all the address entries that follow it, until the end of the message or until another next hop entry appears. Its route tag and prefix length must be set to zero when sending and are ignored on receipt. A next hop of 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:0 means the router that sent the advertisement. A next hop address must be link-local, and if it is not, it is treated as all zeros. The entry is advisory: ignoring it may give a sub-optimal but still valid route.

How many entries fit in one message depends on the MTU of the medium. The RFC gives the number of entries as the space left after the IPv6 header, the UDP header and the RIPng header, divided by the 20-byte entry size.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RIPng message is a 4-byte header followed by a list of 20-byte route entries. The header says whether the message asks for routes or carries them. Each entry gives an IPv6 address prefix, the number of significant bits in that prefix and a cost from 1 to 15, where 16 means the destination is unreachable.

sections.title: Prefixes and Default Routes
sections.content:
RIPng does not need to distinguish between network, subnet and host routes, because an IPv6 address prefix is unambiguous on its own.

Any prefix with a prefix length of zero designates a default route. The RFC suggests using the prefix 0:0:0:0:0:0:0:0 for it, though the prefix itself is essentially ignored. A default route is useful when it is not convenient to list every possible network in the updates and when one or more routers are prepared to handle traffic to networks that are not listed explicitly. Those routers use the default route for every datagram they have no explicit route for.

How a router becomes a default router is left to the implementor. In general the administrator is given a way to say which routers should create and advertise default route entries, and to choose the metric for the default route, so that a precedence can be set among several default routers. Default route entries are then handled by RIPng exactly like any other destination prefix. The RFC advises administrators to make sure that default routes do not propagate further than intended, and notes that default routes should generally not leave the boundary of an Autonomous System. It does not specify a mechanism for enforcing that restriction.
sections.plainLanguage: RIPng does not need to tell networks apart from hosts, because an IPv6 prefix says how much of the address is the network part. A prefix length of zero means the default route: send anything you have no other route for to this router.

sections.title: Timers and Route Expiry
sections.content:
Every 30 seconds the RIPng process wakes up and sends an unsolicited Response message with its complete routing table to every neighbouring router. Because many routers on a single network tend to synchronise with each other, implementations are required to take one of two precautions: use a clock whose rate is not affected by system load, or offset the 30-second timer by a random time of up to 15 seconds in either direction. The offset is derived from half the update period.

Each route has two timers. When the timeout expires, after 180 seconds without an update for that route, the route is no longer valid, but it is kept for a while so that neighbours can be told it has gone. When the garbage-collection timer expires, the route is finally removed from the routing table. The timeout is initialised when a route is established and again every time an update for that route arrives.

A route is deleted when the timeout expires or when an update from the current router sets its metric to 16. In both cases the garbage-collection timer is set for 120 seconds, the metric is set to 16 so the route leaves service, the route change flag is set, and the output process is signalled to send a response. Until the garbage-collection timer expires the route stays in all updates, so that neighbours learn it is gone. If a new route to the same network is established while the garbage-collection timer is running, the new route replaces the one that was about to be deleted and the timer is cleared.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router sends its full route list every 30 seconds, with a random offset so that routers on the same network do not all speak at once. A route that is not refreshed for 180 seconds is marked unreachable, and it stays in the updates for another 120 seconds so that neighbours learn it has gone before it is deleted.

sections.title: Handling Requests and Responses
sections.content:
A Request asks for a response containing all or part of a router's routing table. Requests are normally sent as multicasts from the RIPng port by routers that have just come up and want to fill their tables quickly. If a request has exactly one entry, with a destination prefix of zero, a prefix length of zero and a metric of infinity, it means send the entire routing table. Otherwise each entry is looked up in the routing table, the metric of any matching route is put into the entry, and infinity is used when no route exists.

Whole-table replies get normal Split Horizon processing, but replies to a request for specific entries do not, because the RFC expects those requests to come from diagnostic software that wants the exact contents of the table.

A Response is checked carefully before it is used. It must come from the RIPng port, and its source must be a link-local address. A router must ignore its own output, because a broadcast network can deliver a copy of the router's own multicast straight back to it. Periodic advertisements must arrive with a hop count of 255, which guarantees that the sender is a neighbour, since any intermediate node would have decremented the count. Each entry is then validated: the prefix must not be multicast or link-local, the prefix length must be between 0 and 128, and the metric must be between 1 and 16. An entry that fails a check is ignored and the event logged.

For a valid entry the router computes metric = MIN (metric + cost, infinity), where the cost is that of the network the message arrived on. A route that does not exist is added, unless the metric is infinity. An existing route is replaced when the update comes from the same router with a different metric, or when the new metric is lower. If the new metric equals the old one, the RFC offers an optional heuristic: switch to the new route when the existing route's timeout is at least halfway to its expiry point, instead of waiting for the timeout.

Responses are sent by multicast to the group FF02::9, the all-rip-routers group, on every connected network that supports broadcasting or is a point-to-point link. When a route metric changes, a triggered update follows after a random delay of 1 to 5 seconds, and it need only include the routes whose change flag is set.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that has just started asks its neighbours for their whole route list. It ignores any answer that does not come from a neighbour, then keeps the route with the lower cost. When a cost changes, it tells its neighbours again within a few seconds instead of waiting for the next 30-second update.

sections.title: Split Horizon and Poisoned Reverse
sections.content:
Split Horizon avoids problems caused by sending a route back to the router it was learned from. The basic form omits those routes from the updates sent to that neighbour. On a broadcast network, all routes learned from any neighbour on that network are omitted from the updates sent on it.

Split Horizon with Poisoned Reverse still includes those routes but sets their metric to infinity, so the sender is told that the destination is not reachable through it. The RFC calls this the preferred method of operation, but it asks implementations to provide a per-interface control that allows no horizoning, split horizoning or poisoned reverse to be selected.

Split Horizon applies to triggered updates as well as to regular ones. If a changed route looks unchanged on a network after Split Horizon processing, for example because it now shows an infinite metric, the route need not be sent on that network at all. If no route needs to be sent there, the update may be omitted.
sections.plainLanguage: Split Horizon stops a router from sending a route back to the neighbour it learned it from, because that neighbour would then think the route runs through the sender. Poisoned Reverse sends the route anyway, but with a cost of infinity, which tells the neighbour the destination is not reachable that way.

sections.title: Administrative Controls and Security
sections.content:
Section 3 of the RFC describes administrative controls that are not part of the protocol itself, but that the RFC strongly recommends including in every implementation. They are meant for networks whose routing may be unstable or subject to errors. Two examples are given. A neighbor list lets the administrator name the routers that each router will accept responses from, and a similar list for the routers it sends responses to. By default no restrictions are defined. A filter lists destination prefixes to allow or to disallow, associated with a particular interface in the incoming or the outgoing direction. If a list of allowed prefixes is given, all others are disallowed; if a list of disallowed prefixes is given, all others are allowed. By default no filters are applied.

For security, the RFC says only that RIPng runs over IPv6 and relies on the IP Authentication Header and the IP Encapsulating Security Payload to give routing exchanges integrity and authentication or confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: RIPng has no protection of its own. The RFC expects the security of the layer below, IPv6, to protect routing exchanges. It also suggests optional controls such as a list of trusted neighbours and filters on which destinations may be advertised.
